::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What this lesson is for

Until now you have looked at your **whole** table. But usually you want just a part of it — only your own
district, only the big catches, or only a few columns.

This lesson gives you three simple commands to do that: **list the values** in a column, **keep only the
rows** you want, and **keep only the columns** you want. At the end you will also learn **what to do when
something goes wrong** — because it will, and it is easy to fix.

Press **Run** on each box. Remember: **you cannot break anything.**
:::

## First, one question from last time

Before we start, bring back the most important thing from the last lesson. There is no penalty for a
wrong answer, and remembering it yourself makes the rest of this lesson easier.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof recall_row = Inputs.radio(
  ["One fishing trip", "One kind of fish from one trip", "One fisher"],
  { label: "In your table, what is one row?" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`${
  // `== null` on purpose: Inputs.radio starts at null, not undefined, when nothing is picked.
  recall_row == null
    ? '<div class="alert alert-light py-2">Pick an answer above.</div>'
    : recall_row === "One kind of fish from one trip"
      ? '<div class="alert alert-success py-2"><strong>Yes.</strong> One row is one kind of fish from one trip. A trip that landed three kinds of fish fills three rows, and they all share the same <code>trip_id</code>.</div>'
      : '<div class="alert alert-warning py-2"><strong>Not quite — and this one matters.</strong> One row is <strong>one kind of fish from one trip</strong>, not a whole trip and not one fisher. A trip that landed three kinds of fish fills three rows, sharing one <code>trip_id</code>.</div>'
}`
```

## Before we start

These commands come from a free toolkit called **dplyr**. It is already switched on for you.

{{< include _before-we-start.qmd >}}

## What values are in a column?

Before you can ask for "only one district", you need to know which districts exist. **`distinct()`** lists
each value in a column **once**, leaving out the repeats. Press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
distinct(example, gaul_2_name)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** just **Shimoni** and **Vanga**. Even though Shimoni is on three rows, it is
listed once. This is also how you find the **exact spelling** of a value to use in the next step.
:::

Now on your own data. These are the real districts in your records. Press **Run**, then try changing
`gaul_2_name` to `gear` to see your fishing methods:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
distinct(landings, gaul_2_name)
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Keep this list in view.** These are your own names, spelled exactly as your data spells them. You will
copy one of them further down the page.
:::

## Show only the rows you want

**`filter()`** keeps only the rows that match a condition you give — for example, only the `gillnet`
trips.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
Two small things to get right:

- Use **two** equals signs `==` for "is equal to" (one `=` means something else and will not work).
- A word like `"gillnet"` needs **quotes**. A number, like `5`, does not.
:::

**First, have a guess.** Look back at the little `example` table at the top of the page. It has **5
rows**. Now think about what `filter(example, gear == "gillnet")` will give back.

Guessing first is not a test. It is the fastest way to understand what a command does, and a wrong guess
teaches you more than a right one.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof predict_filter = Inputs.radio(
  ["1 row", "2 rows", "5 rows"],
  { label: "How many rows will come back?" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`${
  // `== null` on purpose: Inputs.radio starts at null, not undefined, when nothing is picked.
  predict_filter == null
    ? '<div class="alert alert-light py-2">Pick an answer above, then press Run below to check it.</div>'
    : predict_filter === "2 rows"
      ? '<div class="alert alert-success py-2"><strong>Yes — 2 rows.</strong> Only two rows have <code>gillnet</code> in the <code>gear</code> column, so only those two are kept. Press <strong>Run</strong> and see.</div>'
      : '<div class="alert alert-warning py-2"><strong>Have another look.</strong> Count the rows in the table above where <code>gear</code> says <code>gillnet</code> — that is how many you will get. A wrong guess is useful: it shows you exactly what to look at.</div>'
}`
```

Now press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
filter(example, gear == "gillnet")
```

```{=html}
<div class="diagram">
<table class="table">
  <thead><tr><th>gaul_2_name</th><th>gear</th><th>catch_taxon</th><th>catch_kg</th></tr></thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr class="drop"><td>Shimoni</td><td>hand line</td><td>species 1</td><td>12</td></tr>
    <tr class="drop"><td>Shimoni</td><td>hand line</td><td>species 2</td><td>5</td></tr>
    <tr class="drop"><td>Shimoni</td><td>hand line</td><td>species 3</td><td>3</td></tr>
    <tr class="keep"><td>Vanga</td><td>gillnet</td><td>species 1</td><td>8</td></tr>
    <tr class="keep"><td>Vanga</td><td>gillnet</td><td>species 2</td><td>6</td></tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
</div>
```
[`filter(gear == "gillnet")` keeps the green rows and drops the rest.]{.diagram-caption}

You can also filter on a **number** — no quotes needed. This keeps only catches heavier than 5 kg:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
filter(example, catch_kg > 5)
```

Now on your real data. This keeps only the catches heavier than 20 kg — the big ones. Press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
filter(landings, catch_kg > 20)
```

### Your turn: your own district

Now you do one. In the box below, replace the blanks `______` with **one district name from your own
list** further up the page. Keep the quotes. Then press **Run**.

If you get stuck, press **Hint**. Nothing here can break.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_filter_district
#| envir: global
#| caption: "Keep only the rows from your own district"
filter(landings, gaul_2_name == "______")
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_filter_district" }
Scroll up to the `distinct(landings, gaul_2_name)` box and copy one name **exactly** as it is spelled
there, between the quotes. For example, if your list shows `Kilifi`, you would write
`filter(landings, gaul_2_name == "Kilifi")`.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_filter_district" }
Any district from your own list works. With a district called `Kilifi` it would be:

```r
filter(landings, gaul_2_name == "Kilifi")
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** only the rows for that one district.

If you get an **empty** table, the name is probably spelled differently in your data. Go back to the
`distinct()` list and copy it again, exactly.
:::

## When the answer comes back red

Now that you are typing, sooner or later you will press **Run** and get **red text** instead of a table.
This happens to everyone, every day, including the people who wrote these lessons.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Red text is not damage.** Nothing is broken, nothing is lost, and your real data cannot be changed from
this page. Red text is simply R saying: *"I did not understand one word."*

You do not need to read all of it. Look for the **last line** — that is the useful one.
:::

Almost every red message you will meet is one of just **two**. Here is each one, and what to do.

### "object ... not found"

This means R met a name it does not recognise. There are two common reasons.

**The name is spelled differently from your data.** The box below has a mistake on purpose. Press **Run**
to see the red text, then **fix the spelling** and press **Run** again.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| error: true
# `geer` is not a column. Fix it, then press Run again.
filter(example, geer == "gillnet")
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** a red line ending in `object 'geer' not found`. R is telling you the name it
could not find — `geer`. Change it to `gear` and the table comes back.

When this happens on your own data, check the real spelling with `names(landings)`, or with the
`distinct()` list further up the page.
:::

**A word is missing its quotes.** `filter(example, gear == gillnet)` gives the *same* message,
`object 'gillnet' not found`. Without quotes, R thinks `gillnet` is the name of a column.

Words always need quotes, like `"gillnet"`. Numbers never do, like `5`.

### "We detected a named input"

This one means you typed **one** `=` where **two** are needed. Press **Run** to see it, then fix it.

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
#| error: true
# One = instead of two. Fix it, then press Run again.
filter(example, gear = "gillnet")
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**What you should see:** red text saying R detected a *named input*, and suggesting you meant `==`. It is
right. Change the single `=` to `==` and press **Run**.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Two ways out, always

- **Edit and press Run again.** You can do this as many times as you like.
- **Press "Start Over"** on the box to put the original instruction back, exactly as it was when the page
  opened.

You cannot get stuck, and you cannot break anything.
:::

## Keep only the columns you want

Your table has many columns. Often you want just a few — say the date, the district and the weight.
**`select()`** keeps only the columns you name:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
select(example, landing_date, gaul_2_name, catch_kg)
```

```{=html}
<div class="col-chips diagram">
  Keep: <span class="keep">landing_date</span><span class="keep">gaul_2_name</span><span class="keep">catch_kg</span>
  &#160;&#160; Drop: <span class="drop">trip_id</span><span class="drop">gear</span><span class="drop">catch_taxon</span>
</div>
```
[`select()` keeps the green columns and leaves out the rest.]{.diagram-caption}

On your real data, keep just three useful columns. Press **Run**, then try adding another column name:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
select(landings, landing_date, gaul_2_name, catch_kg)
```

## Do two steps at once: the pipe `|>`

Most real questions need two steps: keep only **your** district, **and** keep only a few columns. The little
symbol **`|>`** (called the *pipe*) lets you do steps **in order**, left to right. Read it as the word
**"then"**.

The box below says: *take the landings, **then** keep only the catches over 20 kg, **then** keep these
three columns.* Press **Run**:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
landings |>
  filter(catch_kg > 20) |>
  select(landing_date, gaul_2_name, catch_kg)
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
This is the kind of question you will ask most often: **narrow the rows, then narrow the columns.**

Try changing the `20` to a bigger number and pressing **Run** again — fewer rows come back. Or swap the
first step for your own district, the way you did in the exercise above.
:::

## What you have learned

- **`distinct(table, column)`** — list the values in a column once (find your districts, gears, …).
- **`filter(table, condition)`** — keep only the rows that match (use `==`, and quotes for words).
- **`select(table, columns…)`** — keep only the columns you name.
- **`|>`** ("then") — do several steps in order.

And when the answer comes back **red**:

- `object ... not found` — a name is spelled wrong, or a word is missing its quotes.
- `named input` — you typed one `=` where you need two, `==`.
- Either way: edit and press **Run** again, or press **Start Over**. Nothing is broken.

Next: **Add it up** — totals and averages by district, gear or month.
